definition: Optimal matching is a sequence analysis method used in social science, to assess the dissimilarity of ordered arrays of tokens that usually represent a time-ordered sequence of socio-economic states two individuals have experienced.
details: Once such distances have been calculated for a set of observations (e.g. individuals in a cohort) classical tools (such as cluster analysis) can be used. The method was tailored to social sciences from a technique originally introduced to study molecular biology (protein or genetic) sequences (see sequence alignment). Optimal matching uses the Needleman-Wunsch algorithm.

explainer.lead: It is a sequence analysis method used in social science to measure how dissimilar two time-ordered sequences of states are. It matters for comparing life-course trajectories across individuals.

tiers.eli5: It lines up two people's life histories side by side and counts how much editing it takes to turn one into the other.
tiers.practitioner: Researchers compute pairwise distances between observed sequences and then apply classical tools such as cluster analysis; the choice of edit costs shapes the resulting distances.
tiers.paperLevel: Uses the Needleman-Wunsch algorithm, adapted from molecular sequence alignment, to compute dissimilarity between ordered arrays of tokens representing socio-economic states. Distances feed into cluster analysis.

explainer.example: Two individuals' sequences of employment states are compared, and the edit operations needed to turn one sequence into the other give their distance.
